newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand sells itself as low-cost holiday venue.
newsitem.headline: Thailand sells itself as low-cost holiday venue.

text.p: Thailand hopes to use its weak currency to win back foreign tourists in a two-year "Amazing Thailand" promotion which it believes will earn the country one trillion baht ($32 billion), a senior tourism official said on Thursday.

Pradech Phayakvichien, deputy governor of the Tourism Authority of Thailand, told Reuters in an interview he expected more than 17 million foreign tourists in 1998 and 1999, earning the country 600 billion baht ($19 billion) in much-needed foreign currency.
Thailand will also aim to promote domestic tourism, bringing in an estimated 400 billion baht ($13 billion) during the same period.
"I hope the project will help tremendously when the economy is facing a sharp downturn. With the weaker baht, it would be attractive to come to Thailand," Pradech said.

Thailand's economy has gone from boom to bust in recent years, triggering a crisis in which the financial sector has been thrown into turmoil by the fallout from misallocated resources and speculation.
The Thai baht has dropped more than 20 percent since July 2 after the authority scrapped a tightly controlled exchange regime and replaced it with a new managed float system.
Tourism, once one of the country's biggest bread-winners, recently lost its glomour as the government turned its attention to export-oriented and looser financial industries.

From 1988, when the country launched 'Visit Thailand Year', until the Gulf War in 1991 tourism enjoyed double-digit growth but tough competition from regional neighbours, a lack of proper promotion and concerns over AIDS have taken their toll.
The country recorded growth of only four percent in tourism last year.
Nevertheless, the average revenue from tourism accounted for around 4.38 percent of GDP during 1991-1995.
"Unlike other industries which need substantial investment on restructuring to stay competitive, we already have all the resources necessary to make this industry boom again," Pradech said.

He said the tourism authority would promote traditional events and culture as well as foods, handicraft and herbal medicine as selling points, stressing that Thailand will encourage more women and family groups to visit the country.

"We realised the perception of some tourists toward Thailand. Of course, we do have problems about prostitutes, both child or adult. But we are in the process of solving that problem and in no way will we promote such a thing," he said.
"Thailand has much more to offer than that. And it is not true that this country is not a place for female visitors. We will prove that to the world," he said.
